Thoronet
toh-roh-NAY
n. (a Cistercian abbey in the wooded hills of Provence, founded in the 1130s and built about 1160-1190)
From Provençal, probably a diminutive related to a hill or height; the abbey is named from its locality, Le Thoronet.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Le Thoronet is the oldest of the three Cistercian sisters of Provence, settled in the 1130s and built between about 1160 and 1190 in bare local limestone. It is the most severe building of the three and the most famous among architects: its unadorned volumes and extraordinary acoustic — a long reverberation that forces the choir to sing slowly and together — were studied by Le Corbusier, and the abbey has become a standard text in the argument that restraint can be more eloquent than ornament. A Protestant can agree with the aesthetic judgment and still ask the prior question, which is what the building is for. Stone cannot praise and cannot hear. “The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork” (Psa 19:1) gives creation a voice of its own; and Christ's remark about the stones is a rebuke to men, not a promise to masonry: “I tell you that, if these should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out” (Luk 19:40). The acoustic is a servant of the singers, and a church is “built up a spiritual house” (1Pe 2:5) out of people.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines acoustic as pertaining to the ears, to the sense of hearing, or to the doctrine of sounds; echo as a sound reflected or reverberated from a solid body; and stone as a concretion of earthy or mineral matter.

expand to see more

ACOUSTIC, a. Pertaining to the ears, to the sense of hearing, or to the doctrine of sounds.

ECHO, n. A sound reflected or reverberated from a solid body; sound returned; repercussion of sound.

REVERBERATE, v.t. To return, as sound; to send back; to echo.

STONE, n. A concretion of earthy or mineral matter; also, a small mass of such matter.

SIMPLICITY, n. Singleness; the state of being unmixed or uncompounded; plainness; artlessness; freedom from ornament.

Key Scripture

Psa 19:1 — "To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David. The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork."

Luk 19:40 — "And he answered and said unto them, I tell you that, if these should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out."

1Pe 2:5 — "Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ."

Hab 2:20 — "But the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him."

Modern Corruption

The severest of the Provencal Cistercian houses, famous for its acoustic: eloquent restraint in stone, which still cannot praise and cannot hear.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is reverence of the kind a long reverberation enforces: “But the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him” (Hab 2:20). An acoustic that punishes haste is doing a congregation a service, and most modern rooms are built to do the opposite.

The live misuse is the architectural one — Le Thoronet admired as pure form by people indifferent to the psalms it was shaped to carry. The building is a servant and the singers are the church: “Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood” (1Pe 2:5) puts the living stones in the walls and the quarried ones underfoot.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew eben (H68), a stone; Hebrew damam (H1826), to be silent; Greek lithos (G3037), a stone; Greek siopao (G4623), to keep silence; Hebrew heykal (H1964), a temple.

expand to see more

Hebrew eben (H68) — a stone; the material, and in Scripture also a memorial and a cornerstone.

Hebrew damam (H1826) — to be still, to be silent; “let all the earth keep silence before him” (Hab 2:20).

Greek lithos (G3037) — a stone; “the stones would immediately cry out” (Luk 19:40).

Greek lithos zon — a living stone; “as lively stones” (1Pe 2:5) is Peter's phrase for Christians.

Hebrew heykal (H1964) — a palace or temple; the house a congregation now is.

Usage

"“But the LORD is in his holy temple” (Hab 2:20) — the reverence the building was shaped for."

"“the firmament sheweth his handywork” (Psa 19:1) — creation's own eloquence, above any architecture."

"“built up a spiritual house” (1Pe 2:5) — the only masonry that matters."
